videos.t: Single chip (PIC only) DIY retro game console
videos.desc:
This is the open software and open hardware project. The hardware contains one PIC24 microcontroller, small voltage regulator, a few transistors and passive components. There are connectors for VGA monitor, PC speakers, 5V power supply and RS232 (optional) for later firmware upgrade.
The game does not run on PC, so it was recorded by camera. That's why the picture quality is not perfect.
Detailed DIY instructions at http://www.voja.rs/PROJECTS/npr.htm

I made this animation with 16mm Bolex camera in single shot mode, and monochrome monitor. Graphic unit was  my DIY project, made of 2114 RAMs (1Kx4bits, total of 90 chips), Z80A microprocessor and about 40 TTL chips. Resolution was 300x400 (3-bit pixel), and I wrote the software in TRS80 L2 BASIC. There was the solenoid and interface which automated the whole process (1.erase - 2.render - 3.shoot the single frame - go to 1). It took about 24 hours to record this.

This is the very unusual clock, but the good hacker can read its time.
All "bugs" (waveshape shaking and colour blinking) are simulated by software, so it tells the story about hard hacker's work

Rf Dice reading for Sic Bo
videos.desc: This dice reader was developed for SicBo casino game. Accelerometer detects dice number and possible irregular (jam) position. Tilt switches are used to wake the controller from sleep. Battery endurance is about 500,000 cycles.

There are two PIC24EP512GP806 MCUs, one of them controls the mechanical parts and communicates with server, and the other one digitizes the signal from TV camera, locates and recognises the number and generates VGA output (for calibrating and maintenance only). This is stand-alone OCR unit and works independently of PC. One ball cycle is about 1 sec.

This is my new clock. It uses a custom vector TT font and Bezier curves to create a low-resolution anti-aliased bitmap. A 32-bit PRNG creates deformations that are virtually never repeated. As you can see, the digits are not simply replaced, but organically morphed. All of this, including the matrix refresh, is done by a PIC24EP256GP204 at 120 MHz.
